screens.title: Inheritance & Polymorphism in Solidity
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will master how Solidity lets one contract inherit behavior from another, so you can centralize logic and reduce duplication. We will walk through why inheritance matters for access control, pausing mechanisms, and layered features, and you'll see concrete examples such as an Owned base contract and an Advanced contract that composes Pausable behavior. You will learn the exact role of the virtual and override keywords, how to call parent implementations with super, and how constructor arguments are chained across base contracts. I will also highlight common mistakes that introduce vulnerabilities: forgetting to mark functions virtual, incorrectly removing an access modifier when overriding, and state variable shadowing. By the end you'll be able to design a multi-level hierarchy that preserves security properties and uses Solidity's linearization rules to predict behavior. Think of this chapter as both a recipe and a checklist for inheritance: readable, testable, and safe contract composition. As you proceed, reflect on where code reuse will reduce maintenance while keeping access checks intact.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Inheritance & Polymorphism
Inheritance & Polymorphism in Solidity
Create modular contracts, control overrides, and avoid common inheritance vulnerabilities.

This chapter focuses on practical rules: declare base functions virtual to allow overrides, use override in derived contracts, call parent logic with super when you need it, and pass constructor arguments explicitly when needed. Multiple inheritance follows Solidity's C3 linearization so order matters.

screens.title: What is inheritance in Solidity?
screens.narratorSegment: Inheritance in Solidity means a contract can acquire public and internal functions and state variables from another contract, creating a derived contract that behaves as the base plus any additions. The is keyword declares a relationship where the derived contract implicitly contains the base's members. For example, an Owned contract defines owner state and an onlyOwner modifier; any contract that declares is Owned receives that owner state and modifier automatically. Constructors in base contracts still run when you deploy the derived contract, which lets base initialization occur before derived initialization. This matters because correct initialization is often a security property—setting the initial owner or paused flag must happen reliably. A common misconception is that inheritance copies code textually; it does not duplicate state variables into separate storage slots unless you intentionally shadow them. Shadowing occurs when a derived contract declares a state variable with the same name as a base; it creates a distinct variable and leads to confusing behavior. A concrete example: define Owned with owner set to msg. sender in the constructor, then declare contract MyContract is Owned. Deploying MyContract will call Owned's constructor and set owner to the deployer. As you design hierarchies, prefer composition for unrelated cross-cutting concerns, and inheritance when you need to share access checks or lifecycle hooks safely. What base contracts in your next design should centralize access rules?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › What is inheritance?
Quick Definition

Inheritance lets a derived contract acquire public and internal state and functions from base contracts using the is keyword. Constructors of bases run during deployment.

Common misconception: inheritance copies storage. In reality, declaration and shadowing determine storage layout; duplicate names create separate variables.
Concrete example
// Owned base
contract Owned {
  address public owner;
  constructor() { owner = msg.sender; }
  modifier onlyOwner() { require(msg.sender==owner, "Caller is not the owner"); _; }
}

contract MyContract is Owned {
  uint public value;
  constructor(uint _initialValue) { value = _initialValue; }
}
Explanation & implications
  • Base constructors run first, ensuring shared state like owner is set before derived logic.
  • Inherited modifiers such as onlyOwner can be combined with new modifiers in derived contracts.
  • Avoid shadowing state variables; it creates separate storage and confusion.
Key Takeaway

Inheritance centralizes shared behavior but requires explicit constructor handling and careful storage design.

screens.title: Owned contract and modifiers
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the Owned contract, a minimal pattern you'll encounter often. The contract stores an owner address, sets it in the constructor to the deployer, and exposes an onlyOwner modifier that gates sensitive functions. This pattern centralizes authority checks so derived contracts can inherit and reuse them. In practice, when you write functions that change critical state, you apply onlyOwner to prevent unauthorized calls. A common pitfall is assuming inherited modifiers are automatically secure if the derived contract later overrides functions without preserving the modifier. If you override an owner-only function and forget to include onlyOwner in the derived implementation, you remove that protection and introduce a security hole. Another subtle point: the Owned constructor runs during derived deployment, so the deployer becomes owner of the derived contract unless you explicitly reassign owner in a chained constructor. As an example, MyContract is Owned inherits owner and onlyOwner; its constructor calls Owned implicitly and owner becomes the deployer. When testing, always assert the owner address and try restricted calls from non-owner accounts to verify the modifier. For practice, consider adding a transferOwnership function and check that onlyOwner controls it. What test would you write first to validate ownership?

keyIdea.title: Owned pattern
keyIdea.text: OnlyOwner centralizes authority checks; ensure overrides preserve access control to avoid vulnerabilities.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Owned & modifiers
Owned contract (example)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract Owned {
  address public owner;
  constructor() { owner = msg.sender; }
  modifier onlyOwner() {
    require(msg.sender == owner, "Caller is not the owner");
    _;
  }
  function transferOwnership(address _newOwner) public onlyOwner {
    require(_newOwner != address(0), "New owner cannot be the zero address");
    owner = _newOwner;
  }
}
Explanation
  • The modifier enforces that only the owner can run guarded functions.
  • Because Derived inherits Owned, it gets owner and onlyOwner without extra code.
  • Overriding an onlyOwner function must retain or strengthen the access check.
Common Mistake

Removing onlyOwner in an override effectively opens access to sensitive operations. Always re-apply or call parent's guarded logic.

screens.title: Constructor chaining and argument passing
screens.narratorSegment: Constructor chaining determines how base contracts initialize their state when a derived contract is deployed. Solidity executes base constructors in the order defined by its linearization, and if a base constructor requires arguments you must pass them explicitly from the derived constructor. For example, if Base(uint v) requires a value, you declare contract Derived is Base and write constructor(uint v) Base(v) { /* derived init */ }. Forgetting to pass arguments leads to compilation errors or unintended defaults. Another key point: the order of contracts in the is clause affects execution order when multiple inheritance is present, so place base contracts in an order that matches your intent for initialization. A typical mistake is relying on implicit default constructors when a base actually needs an explicit value; the compiler forces you to resolve this, which is a beneficial safety. In practice, test deployment paths for each constructor signature combination and verify critical state like owner, paused, or role assignments. For robust design, prefer explicit constructor argument passing and document which base expects what. Ask yourself: does any base contract require a runtime parameter that the derived contract must provide?

keyIdea.title: Constructor chaining
keyIdea.text: Always pass required arguments to base constructors explicitly to ensure predictable initialization across inheritance chains.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Constructor chaining
Pattern
contract Base {
  uint public x;
  constructor(uint _x) { x = _x; }
}

contract Derived is Base {
  constructor(uint _v) Base(_v) {
    // Derived init
  }
}
Checklist
  • Identify which bases require constructor arguments.
  • Pass those arguments in the derived constructor signature using Base(arg).
  • Confirm the order of bases in the is clause matches intended initialization order.
Key Takeaway

Explicit constructor argument passing prevents runtime surprises and enforces correct base initialization.

screens.title: virtual vs override
screens.narratorSegment: Polymorphism in Solidity is explicit: the base must mark a function virtual to allow overrides, and the derived must declare override to replace that implementation. This explicitness prevents accidental replacements but requires you to be deliberate when designing extensible base contracts. For instance, Pausable. pause marked virtual signals designers that derived contracts might augment pause behavior. The derived contract then writes function pause() public override onlyOwner { super. pause(); } to both restrict access and retain parent logic. A common misconception is thinking override alone is enough; without virtual in the base, the compiler will raise an error. Another misconception is that overriding always replaces the parent entirely. Using super lets you reuse parent logic instead of discarding it. In multiple inheritance, override requires listing all bases if multiple define the same function signature. The practical rule is: declare virtual only when you expect derivation, use override to be explicit, and call super when preservation of parent behavior is required. Consider whether the derived implementation should strengthen, not weaken, access and invariants. Which of your base functions should be sealed and which should be virtual?

keyIdea.title: Polymorphism rules
keyIdea.text: virtual enables replacement; override signals the new implementation; use super to combine behaviors rather than drop parent logic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › virtual vs override
Example
contract Pausable {
  bool public paused;
  constructor() { paused = false; }
  function pause() public virtual { paused = true; }
  function unpause() public virtual { paused = false; }
}

contract Advanced is Pausable, Owned {
  function pause() public override onlyOwner { super.pause(); }
}
Notes
  • Mark base functions virtual only when you expect safe overrides.
  • Derived functions must list override and can still call super to reuse parent logic.
  • In multiple inheritance, list all bases in override if function exists in several bases.
Pitfall

Removing or weakening access control in an override introduces critical vulnerabilities. Strengthen or preserve, never weaken.

screens.title: Multiple inheritance and C3 linearization
screens.narratorSegment: Solidity supports multiple inheritance, letting a contract inherit from multiple bases. To avoid ambiguity when multiple bases define the same function or constructor behavior, Solidity uses a C3 linearization algorithm to determine a consistent order. Practically, this means the order you list base contracts in the is clause affects which base constructor runs first and how overridden functions are resolved. For example, contract Advanced is Owned, Pausable ensures Owned's constructor runs before Pausable's if the linearization orders that way; more complex hierarchies follow the C3 rules to produce a single deterministic order. A common source of bugs is the diamond problem, where two bases inherit from a common ancestor and the derived contract ends up with multiple paths to that ancestor. Solidity's linearization prevents duplicate ancestor initialization but you must still reason about which implementation will be used when multiple bases define the same function signature. When designing hierarchies, prefer simple trees over deep diamonds, document the intended resolution, and write explicit override implementations that call super with the desired chain of parent logic. For safety, add tests verifying constructor side effects and the identity of state variables after deployment. How would you reorder bases to change initialization order when needed?

screens.title: Polymorphic override with super
screens.narratorSegment: Overriding a function gives derived contracts the power to change behavior, but often you need to preserve the parent's logic and add constraints. The super keyword calls the next implementation in the linearized inheritance chain and is useful when the derived needs to extend, not replace, functionality. For example, Pausable. pause might simply set a boolean. AdvancedMyContract overrides pause to add onlyOwner and then calls super. pause so the boolean change still happens. This pattern preserves invariants established by the base while allowing derived contracts to inject access control or logging. A trap is calling parent's logic after changing state in ways that invalidate parent assumptions; prefer calling super either before or after derived checks based on correctness. Additionally, in multiple inheritance super follows the C3 order, so understand which parent implementation you will invoke. A test-driven approach: write a unit test that calls pause as non-owner and as owner, and assert both modifier enforcement and paused state. This confirms you did not accidentally remove base behavior or weaken security. How will you order super calls to preserve invariants in your contract?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › override & super
AdvancedMyContract snippet
contract AdvancedMyContract is Owned, Pausable {
  uint public counter;
  constructor(uint _initialCounter) { counter = _initialCounter; }

  function pause() public override onlyOwner {
    super.pause();
  }

  function unpause() public override onlyOwner {
    super.unpause();
  }

  function increment() public whenNotPaused { counter++; }
}
Practical guidance
  • Use onlyOwner in the override to strengthen access control.
  • Call super to preserve base state changes such as setting paused to true.
  • Test both behavior and access restrictions in unit tests to ensure expectations hold.
Key Takeaway

Combining override and super lets you extend behavior safely while maintaining parent invariants.

screens.title: Polymorphism explained
screens.narratorSegment: Polymorphism means different contracts can respond to the same function signature in their own ways. In Solidity, this is achieved via virtual and override. A base contract declares a function as virtual to indicate that derived contracts may replace it with specialized behavior. Derived contracts then declare override to present their own implementation. This allows, for example, multiple token contracts to implement a standard transfer behavior while each adds custom logging or access controls. Importantly, polymorphism in Solidity is explicit and type-safe: the compiler forces virtual and override declarations so you avoid unintentional replacement. A misconception is assuming polymorphism implies implicit runtime dispatch like some dynamic languages: Solidity's mechanism is compile-time explicit, and function resolution is determined by the inheritance linearization. A concrete example: a base contract provides a getX function virtual, and Derived returns a different value by overriding it and optionally calling super. When you design libraries or frameworks, mark only the functions you intend to be polymorphic and document expected invariants. Consider whether a function should be sealed or open to override based on security and invariants you need to preserve.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Polymorphism
Concept

Different contracts can respond to the same function call in unique ways when a base marks a function virtual and a derived uses override.

Concrete example
A base provides getX virtual; a derived overrides getX to return x + y. This is used to customize behavior while using the same interface.
Misconception check
  • Polymorphism is not implicit dynamic dispatch; it's explicit and resolved via compile-time rules.
  • Only mark functions virtual when you design for extension and can guarantee invariants.
Key Takeaway

Use polymorphism deliberately to provide interchangeable behavior while preserving security and invariants.

screens.title: State variable shadowing & access weakening
screens.narratorSegment: Two common pitfalls in inheritance are state variable shadowing and weakening access controls during overrides. Shadowing happens when a derived contract declares a state variable with the same name as one in a base contract; rather than referring to the same storage slot, you create a new variable in the derived contract. This leads to bugs where code reads one variable while another governs logic, producing inconsistent state that is hard to debug. To avoid this, do not redeclare variables from a base; instead, use inherited variables or rename deliberately. The second pitfall is weakening access control: if a base function is protected by onlyOwner and a derived contract overrides that function without the modifier, you have removed the safety check. Overriding should either preserve the modifier, call the parent's guarded logic via super, or replace it with a stricter check. Never remove a security guard unless you are deliberately restructuring access with full awareness of consequences. The practical guideline: audit overrides for modifiers and storage names, and include unit tests that confirm access restrictions and expected storage values after operations. What test will catch a shadowing mistake early?

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › AccessControl Lab
Starter code (partial)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract AccessControl {
  enum Role { Admin, Editor, Viewer, None }
  mapping(address => Role) private userRoles;

  constructor() { userRoles[msg.sender] = Role.Admin; }

  modifier onlyRole(Role _role) {
    require(userRoles[msg.sender] == _role, "AccessControl: Caller does not have the required role");
    _;
  }

  function grantRole(address _user, Role _role) public virtual onlyRole(Role.Admin) {
    require(_user != address(0), "AccessControl: Cannot grant role to zero address");
    userRoles[_user] = _role;
  }

  function revokeRole(address _user) public virtual onlyRole(Role.Admin) {
    require(_user != address(0), "AccessControl: Cannot revoke role from zero address");
    userRoles[_user] = Role.None;
  }

  function getRole(address _user) public view returns (Role) { return userRoles[_user]; }
}

contract ContentManager is AccessControl {
  string public content;
  // TODO: Implement publishContent and viewContent
  // TODO: Override grantRole to emit RoleGranted after calling super.grantRole()
}
Lab checklist
  • Implement publishContent as onlyRole(Role.Editor).
  • Implement viewContent as onlyRole(Role.Viewer).
  • Override grantRole, call super.grantRole and emit RoleGranted.
  • Write tests: role assignment, publish success/fail, event emission.

screens.title: Assessment: override effects and state changes
screens.narratorSegment: This assessment asks you to analyze a Base and Derived contract where Derived overrides functions and calls super. You must predict final state after invoking methods. For example, Base sets x to 10 and provides virtual modifyX that sets x. Derived overrides modifyX, calls super. modifyX with the new value, and then sets its own y based on the argument. When you call modifyX on Derived and then getX which returns x plus y, you must track both assignments: super. modifyX changes base x, and derived sets y = newX * 2. Working through the steps, if you call modifyX(5), base x becomes 5 and derived y becomes 10, so getX returns 15. This exercise tests your ability to follow constructor and function execution order, super calls, and overridden returns. A typical mistake is assuming base values are unchanged or double-counted; carefully note where super runs and how derived assignments update other state. In practice, draft a table of state transitions for each call to avoid errors. Can you write the minimal unit test that asserts the final values after calling modifyX?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Assessment Example
Example contracts
contract Base {
  uint public x = 10;
  function getX() public virtual view returns (uint) { return x; }
  function modifyX(uint _newX) public virtual { x = _newX; }
}

contract Derived is Base {
  uint public y = 20;
  function getX() public override view returns (uint) { return x + y; }
  function modifyX(uint _newX) public override {
    super.modifyX(_newX);
    y = _newX * 2;
  }
}
State transition table (call modifyX(5))
  1. Initially: x = 10, y = 20.
  2. super.modifyX(5) sets x = 5.
  3. Derived sets y = 10.
  4. getX() returns x + y = 5 + 10 = 15.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will master how Solidity lets one contract inherit behavior from another, so you can centralize logic and reduce duplication. We will walk through why inheritance matters for access control, pausing mechanisms, and layered features, and you'll see concrete examples such as an Owned base contract and an Advanced contract that composes Pausable behavior. You will learn the exact role of the virtual and override keywords, how to call parent implementations with super, and how constructor arguments are chained across base contracts. I will also highlight common mistakes that introduce vulnerabilities: forgetting to mark functions virtual, incorrectly removing an access modifier when overriding, and state variable shadowing. By the end you'll be able to design a multi-level hierarchy that preserves security properties and uses Solidity's linearization rules to predict behavior. Think of this chapter as both a recipe and a checklist for inheritance: readable, testable, and safe contract composition. As you proceed, reflect on where code reuse will reduce maintenance while keeping access checks intact.

These objectives guide our practice and assessments. First, you will understand inheritance fundamentals in Solidity: how the is keyword transfers public and internal state and functions, and why constructor chaining matters. Second, you'll differentiate virtual and override: knowing when a function can be replaced and how to declare overrides safely. Third, you will practice initializing base contracts via constructor arguments to ensure correct state across layers. Fourth, you will identify common pitfalls and adopt best practices, including avoiding state shadowing and not weakening access controls when overriding. Each objective emphasizes both code patterns and security consequences so you can write maintainable contracts and avoid silent vulnerabilities. We'll verify competency with code examples and a hands-on AccessControl exercise. Keep these objectives in mind as you read the examples and work through the starter code: they are both the checklist and the assessment rubric for your design decisions.

These objectives frame practical tasks and the hands-on exercise. You'll implement a multi-level access control system to practice passing constructor parameters and overriding functions safely. The exercise requires using an enum for roles, a mapping to store roles, and modifiers that enforce role checks. You will then inherit that AccessControl in a ContentManager contract, restrict publishing and viewing by role, and override grantRole to emit an event after calling the parent implementation. This enforces the discipline of calling super when preserving base behavior. During assessment, we'll look for correct use of onlyRole, explicit virtual/override when needed, no state shadowing, and unchanged or strengthened access control. Finally, we will review the answers to short conceptual questions about C3 linearization and the difference between super and explicit base calls. These checks ensure you can not only write inheritance code but reason about the security implications of each override.

Inheritance in Solidity means a contract can acquire public and internal functions and state variables from another contract, creating a derived contract that behaves as the base plus any additions. The is keyword declares a relationship where the derived contract implicitly contains the base's members. For example, an Owned contract defines owner state and an onlyOwner modifier; any contract that declares is Owned receives that owner state and modifier automatically. Constructors in base contracts still run when you deploy the derived contract, which lets base initialization occur before derived initialization. This matters because correct initialization is often a security property—setting the initial owner or paused flag must happen reliably. A common misconception is that inheritance copies code textually; it does not duplicate state variables into separate storage slots unless you intentionally shadow them. Shadowing occurs when a derived contract declares a state variable with the same name as a base; it creates a distinct variable and leads to confusing behavior. A concrete example: define Owned with owner set to msg. sender in the constructor, then declare contract MyContract is Owned. Deploying MyContract will call Owned's constructor and set owner to the deployer. As you design hierarchies, prefer composition for unrelated cross-cutting concerns, and inheritance when you need to share access checks or lifecycle hooks safely. What base contracts in your next design should centralize access rules?

Let's walk through the Owned contract, a minimal pattern you'll encounter often. The contract stores an owner address, sets it in the constructor to the deployer, and exposes an onlyOwner modifier that gates sensitive functions. This pattern centralizes authority checks so derived contracts can inherit and reuse them. In practice, when you write functions that change critical state, you apply onlyOwner to prevent unauthorized calls. A common pitfall is assuming inherited modifiers are automatically secure if the derived contract later overrides functions without preserving the modifier. If you override an owner-only function and forget to include onlyOwner in the derived implementation, you remove that protection and introduce a security hole. Another subtle point: the Owned constructor runs during derived deployment, so the deployer becomes owner of the derived contract unless you explicitly reassign owner in a chained constructor. As an example, MyContract is Owned inherits owner and onlyOwner; its constructor calls Owned implicitly and owner becomes the deployer. When testing, always assert the owner address and try restricted calls from non-owner accounts to verify the modifier. For practice, consider adding a transferOwnership function and check that onlyOwner controls it. What test would you write first to validate ownership?

Constructor chaining determines how base contracts initialize their state when a derived contract is deployed. Solidity executes base constructors in the order defined by its linearization, and if a base constructor requires arguments you must pass them explicitly from the derived constructor. For example, if Base(uint v) requires a value, you declare contract Derived is Base and write constructor(uint v) Base(v) { /* derived init */ }. Forgetting to pass arguments leads to compilation errors or unintended defaults. Another key point: the order of contracts in the is clause affects execution order when multiple inheritance is present, so place base contracts in an order that matches your intent for initialization. A typical mistake is relying on implicit default constructors when a base actually needs an explicit value; the compiler forces you to resolve this, which is a beneficial safety. In practice, test deployment paths for each constructor signature combination and verify critical state like owner, paused, or role assignments. For robust design, prefer explicit constructor argument passing and document which base expects what. Ask yourself: does any base contract require a runtime parameter that the derived contract must provide?

Polymorphism in Solidity is explicit: the base must mark a function virtual to allow overrides, and the derived must declare override to replace that implementation. This explicitness prevents accidental replacements but requires you to be deliberate when designing extensible base contracts. For instance, Pausable. pause marked virtual signals designers that derived contracts might augment pause behavior. The derived contract then writes function pause() public override onlyOwner { super. pause(); } to both restrict access and retain parent logic. A common misconception is thinking override alone is enough; without virtual in the base, the compiler will raise an error. Another misconception is that overriding always replaces the parent entirely. Using super lets you reuse parent logic instead of discarding it. In multiple inheritance, override requires listing all bases if multiple define the same function signature. The practical rule is: declare virtual only when you expect derivation, use override to be explicit, and call super when preservation of parent behavior is required. Consider whether the derived implementation should strengthen, not weaken, access and invariants. Which of your base functions should be sealed and which should be virtual?

Solidity supports multiple inheritance, letting a contract inherit from multiple bases. To avoid ambiguity when multiple bases define the same function or constructor behavior, Solidity uses a C3 linearization algorithm to determine a consistent order. Practically, this means the order you list base contracts in the is clause affects which base constructor runs first and how overridden functions are resolved. For example, contract Advanced is Owned, Pausable ensures Owned's constructor runs before Pausable's if the linearization orders that way; more complex hierarchies follow the C3 rules to produce a single deterministic order. A common source of bugs is the diamond problem, where two bases inherit from a common ancestor and the derived contract ends up with multiple paths to that ancestor. Solidity's linearization prevents duplicate ancestor initialization but you must still reason about which implementation will be used when multiple bases define the same function signature. When designing hierarchies, prefer simple trees over deep diamonds, document the intended resolution, and write explicit override implementations that call super with the desired chain of parent logic. For safety, add tests verifying constructor side effects and the identity of state variables after deployment. How would you reorder bases to change initialization order when needed?

Overriding a function gives derived contracts the power to change behavior, but often you need to preserve the parent's logic and add constraints. The super keyword calls the next implementation in the linearized inheritance chain and is useful when the derived needs to extend, not replace, functionality. For example, Pausable. pause might simply set a boolean. AdvancedMyContract overrides pause to add onlyOwner and then calls super. pause so the boolean change still happens. This pattern preserves invariants established by the base while allowing derived contracts to inject access control or logging. A trap is calling parent's logic after changing state in ways that invalidate parent assumptions; prefer calling super either before or after derived checks based on correctness. Additionally, in multiple inheritance super follows the C3 order, so understand which parent implementation you will invoke. A test-driven approach: write a unit test that calls pause as non-owner and as owner, and assert both modifier enforcement and paused state. This confirms you did not accidentally remove base behavior or weaken security. How will you order super calls to preserve invariants in your contract?

Polymorphism means different contracts can respond to the same function signature in their own ways. In Solidity, this is achieved via virtual and override. A base contract declares a function as virtual to indicate that derived contracts may replace it with specialized behavior. Derived contracts then declare override to present their own implementation. This allows, for example, multiple token contracts to implement a standard transfer behavior while each adds custom logging or access controls. Importantly, polymorphism in Solidity is explicit and type-safe: the compiler forces virtual and override declarations so you avoid unintentional replacement. A misconception is assuming polymorphism implies implicit runtime dispatch like some dynamic languages: Solidity's mechanism is compile-time explicit, and function resolution is determined by the inheritance linearization. A concrete example: a base contract provides a getX function virtual, and Derived returns a different value by overriding it and optionally calling super. When you design libraries or frameworks, mark only the functions you intend to be polymorphic and document expected invariants. Consider whether a function should be sealed or open to override based on security and invariants you need to preserve.

Two common pitfalls in inheritance are state variable shadowing and weakening access controls during overrides. Shadowing happens when a derived contract declares a state variable with the same name as one in a base contract; rather than referring to the same storage slot, you create a new variable in the derived contract. This leads to bugs where code reads one variable while another governs logic, producing inconsistent state that is hard to debug. Overriding should either preserve the modifier, call the parent's guarded logic via super, or replace it with a stricter check. Never remove a security guard unless you are deliberately restructuring access with full awareness of consequences. The practical guideline: audit overrides for modifiers and storage names, and include unit tests that confirm access restrictions and expected storage values after operations.
